content.question: What is the primary purpose of TextInputLayout in Android material design?

options.text: It acts as an outer container that adds material design features like floating labels, outline boxes, and error text
It directly handles user text input like EditText
It is used to create buttons with material styling
It replaces the entire LinearLayout for form designs

content.explanation: TextInputLayout acts as an outer container or shell that adds material design features such as floating labels, outline boxes, error text, helper text, counters, and icons. It is not an input field itself — it is a decorative element.
hints: Think of it as a wrapper, not the input itself
It provides visual enhancements around input fields
Floating labels and outline boxes are its key features

content.question: What component must be placed inside TextInputLayout to handle actual user text input?

options.text: TextInputEditText
EditText
TextView
TextInputField

content.explanation: TextInputEditText is a specialised EditText optimised to work with TextInputLayout. It handles the actual text input by the user while TextInputLayout provides the decorative shell.
hints: It's a specialised version of EditText
It's designed to pair with TextInputLayout
Its name includes both 'TextInput' and 'EditText'

content.question: Which attribute is used to set the outline border colour of a TextInputLayout?

options.text: boxStrokeColor
borderColor
outlineColor
strokeTint

content.explanation: The boxStrokeColor attribute sets the colour of the outline border around the TextInputLayout. This colour is applied when the field is focused/active.
hints: The attribute name includes 'box' and 'stroke'
It controls the outline appearance
It's specific to material TextInputLayout

content.question: What does the `boxStrokeWidth` attribute control in TextInputLayout?

options.text: The thickness of the outline border around the input field
The width of the entire TextInputLayout
The padding inside the input field
The margin between text and the border

content.explanation: boxStrokeWidth sets the thickness/width of the outline border stroke. In the lesson, it was set to 2dp to create a visible border around the input field.
hints: It's about the border line itself
Think thickness, not container size
Measured in dp units

content.question: Why does the full package name `com.google.android.material.textfield.TextInputLayout` appear in XML instead of just `TextInputLayout`?

options.text: Because TextInputLayout is part of the Material Design Components library and requires the full qualified name
Because Android Studio cannot auto-detect the component
Because it is a custom component created by the developer
Because short names are not allowed in XML layouts

content.explanation: TextInputLayout belongs to Google's Material Design Components library (com.google.android.material), so the full package path is required in XML. Unlike built-in components like EditText, material components need their fully qualified class name.
hints: It belongs to an external library, not core Android
The package starts with com.google.android.material
Built-in components like EditText don't need this

content.question: What is the floating label animation in TextInputLayout?

options.text: When the field is tapped, the hint text animates upward to become a label above the input
The entire input field floats to the top of the screen
The label disappears when the user starts typing
The label changes colour and stays in place

content.explanation: TextInputLayout provides a floating label animation where the hint text moves up and shrinks into a smaller label above the input when the user clicks on the field. This is a key material design feature.
hints: The hint doesn't disappear — it moves
It goes to the upper side of the field
It's an animation triggered by focus

content.question: How do you override the default inactive border colour of a TextInputLayout?

options.text: Define a colour named `mtrl_textinput_default_box_stroke_color` in colours.xml to replace the material default
Set `boxStrokeColor` to the desired colour — it works for both active and inactive states
Use `android:background` on the TextInputLayout
Set `app:strokeColorInactive` attribute in XML

content.explanation: The boxStrokeColor only applies when the field is active/focused. To change the inactive/default border colour, you must override the material default by defining a colour named `mtrl_textinput_default_box_stroke_color` in your colours.xml file.
hints: boxStrokeColor alone only works when the field is active
You need to override a material default value
It involves changing something in colours.xml

content.question: What attribute is used to set the hint text inside a TextInputLayout?

options.text: android:hint
app:labelText
android:text
app:placeholder

content.explanation: The `android:hint` attribute on TextInputLayout sets the hint/label text that appears inside the field and floats up when the field is focused. For example, `android:hint="Full Name"`.
hints: It's the same attribute used for normal EditText hints
It displays placeholder text before user types
It becomes the floating label when focused

content.question: Which attribute sets the colour of the hint text in TextInputLayout?

options.text: android:textColorHint
app:hintTextColor
android:hintColor
app:labelTextColor

content.explanation: The `android:textColorHint` attribute sets the colour of the hint text displayed in the TextInputLayout. The instructor used this along with `app:hintTextColor` to style the hint in vivid blue.
hints: It starts with android:textColor
It specifically targets the hint text colour
It uses the standard Android namespace

content.question: What is the `inputType` attribute used for in TextInputEditText?

options.text: It specifies the type of data the user can enter, such as text, number, or password
It defines the size of the input field
It sets the font style of the input text
It determines whether the field is editable or read-only

content.explanation: The `inputType` attribute determines what kind of data the user can input and what keyboard is shown. For example, `text` shows a regular keyboard, while `textPassword` masks the input with dots.
hints: It controls the keyboard type and input behaviour
Different values include text, number, textPassword
It affects how the entered text is displayed

content.question: Which attribute enables the password visibility toggle (eye icon) on a TextInputLayout?

options.text: app:passwordToggleEnabled="true"
android:showPassword="true"
app:eyeIconVisible="true"
android:togglePassword="true"

content.explanation: Setting `app:passwordToggleEnabled="true"` on a TextInputLayout adds an eye icon that lets users toggle password visibility between hidden (dots) and visible (plain text).
hints: The attribute uses 'passwordToggle' in its name
It accepts true or false
It belongs to the app namespace, not android

content.question: What does the `app:passwordToggleTint` attribute do?

options.text: Changes the colour of the password toggle eye icon
Changes the colour of the password text
Changes the background colour of the password field
Changes the border colour when password is visible

content.explanation: The `passwordToggleTint` attribute changes the colour of the eye icon used for toggling password visibility. The instructor changed it from the default black to blue (vivid blue).
hints: Tint means applying colour over a surface
It affects the eye icon specifically
It's a colour attribute

content.question: What `inputType` value should be used for a password field in TextInputEditText?

options.text: textPassword
password
text
hiddenText

content.explanation: The `inputType="textPassword"` value masks user input with dots, making it suitable for password fields. Other options like `numberPassword` and `textWebPassword` also exist for specific use cases.
hints: It combines 'text' with 'Password'
It makes the typed characters appear as dots
There are also numberPassword and textWebPassword variants

content.question: What does enabling `app:counterEnabled="true"` on a TextInputLayout do?

options.text: Displays a character count below the input field showing how many characters the user has typed
Limits the total number of characters the user can type
Counts the number of times the user taps the field
Shows the number of words entered by the user

content.explanation: Enabling the counter displays a live character count below the input field (e.g., '0/20'). It shows how many characters have been entered. Combined with `counterMaxLength`, it shows the count relative to the maximum.
hints: It shows a number below the text field
It tracks characters as you type
It works with counterMaxLength to show x/y format

content.question: What does `app:counterMaxLength="20"` specify?

options.text: The maximum character limit displayed in the counter (e.g., 0/20)
The maximum width of the input field in characters
The minimum number of characters required
The font size of the counter text

content.explanation: The `counterMaxLength` attribute sets the maximum number displayed in the counter indicator. When set to 20, the counter shows 'x/20' where x is the current character count. Note: it displays the limit but doesn't enforce it by default.
hints: It sets the number after the slash in the counter
In the lesson, it showed 0/20
It defines the target maximum characters

content.question: How do you initialise a TextInputLayout variable in Kotlin using `findViewById`?

options.text: val fullName: TextInputLayout = findViewById<TextInputLayout>(R.id.fullname)
val fullName: EditText = findViewById<EditText>(R.id.fullname)
val fullName = findViewByName("fullname")
val fullName: TextInputLayout = getComponent(R.id.fullname)

content.explanation: Since the XML component is a TextInputLayout, the type cast must be `TextInputLayout`, not `EditText`. The syntax uses `findViewById<TextInputLayout>(R.id.idName)` to find and cast the view.
hints: The type must match the XML component
It uses findViewById with angle brackets for the type
R.id references the ID set in XML

content.question: How do you collect text from a TextInputLayout in Kotlin?

options.text: fullNameValue.editText?.text.toString()
fullNameValue.text.toString()
fullNameValue.getText()
fullNameValue.inputText.toString()

content.explanation: Unlike EditText where you use `.text.toString()` directly, TextInputLayout requires an extra step: first access `.editText` to get the inner TextInputEditText, then access `.text.toString()`. This is because TextInputLayout is the outer shell, not the input itself.
hints: TextInputLayout is a wrapper — you need to reach the inner component
The keyword 'editText' is used as a property
It's different from how you collect text from a plain EditText

content.question: Why is the text collection syntax different for TextInputLayout compared to EditText?

options.text: Because TextInputLayout is the outer shell and does not hold text directly — you must access its inner editText first
Because TextInputLayout uses a different programming language
Because TextInputLayout automatically converts text to integers
Because TextInputLayout stores text in a database instead of memory

content.explanation: The instructor emphasized that whenever the component changes, the writing style changes too. TextInputLayout is a decorative container; the actual text is held by the TextInputEditText inside it. Hence you need `.editText?.text.toString()` instead of just `.text.toString()`.
hints: Remember: TextInputLayout = outer shell, TextInputEditText = actual input
The text lives in the inner component
Different components require different access patterns

It starts with 'set' and ends with 'Listener'
It creates a block of code that runs on click

Collect values → Set click listener → Assign IDs → Initialise variables

Initialise variables → Collect values → Assign IDs → Set click listener
